---
title: "Expected gain per cycle and per year"
description: "The general gain equation used to compare selection methods."
---

## The idea

Fehr writes the expected genetic gain from one cycle of selection in a general form that covers most methods:

$$
\Delta G = \frac{c\,k\,\sigma^2_A}{\sigma_P}, \qquad \Delta G_{\text{year}} = \frac{c\,k\,\sigma^2_A}{y\,\sigma_P} .
$$

- **k** is the standardized selection differential, the same as Falconer & Mackay's *i*. It depends only on the proportion selected (see [selection intensity](../quantgen/selection-intensity.qmd)).
- **σ²~A~** is the additive genetic variance among the units selected. For families it is the part of σ²~A~ that the family means carry (for example ¼σ²~A~ among half-sib families).
- **σ~P~** is the phenotypic standard deviation among the units selected, which shrinks as testing improves (see [entry-mean heritability](heritability-entry-mean.qmd)).
- **c** is **parental control**: ½ when only the female parent is selected and pollen comes from the whole population, 1 when both parents of the next generation are selected.
- **y** is the number of years per cycle.

Because σ²~A~/σ~P~ = *h*² σ~P~, this is the breeder's equation *R* = *i h*² σ~P~ with two practical additions: who controls pollination, and how long a cycle takes. Gain per year, not gain per cycle, is what decides between methods.

*Source: Fehr, selection theory; Falconer & Mackay, chapter 11.*

## Widget

Set up two selection schemes and compare them. Both start from the same population.

```{ojs}
import {pal, intensity} from "../js/common.js"

viewof vA = Inputs.range([1, 50], {value: 10, step: 1, label: "σ²A among selection units"})
viewof vP = Inputs.range([1, 100], {value: 30, step: 1, label: "σ²P among selection units"})
```

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
**Scheme A**

```{ojs}
viewof pA = Inputs.range([0.01, 0.8], {value: 0.1, step: 0.01, label: "Proportion selected"})
viewof cA = Inputs.radio(new Map([["½ (one parent)", 0.5], ["1 (both parents)", 1]]), {value: 1, label: "Parental control"})
viewof yA = Inputs.range([1, 6], {value: 2, step: 1, label: "Years per cycle"})
```
:::
::: {.column width="4%"}
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
**Scheme B**

```{ojs}
viewof pB = Inputs.range([0.01, 0.8], {value: 0.2, step: 0.01, label: "Proportion selected"})
viewof cB = Inputs.radio(new Map([["½ (one parent)", 0.5], ["1 (both parents)", 1]]), {value: 0.5, label: "Parental control"})
viewof yB = Inputs.range([1, 6], {value: 1, step: 1, label: "Years per cycle"})
```
:::
:::

```{ojs}
scheme = (name, p, c, y) => {
  const k = intensity(p), perCycle = c * k * vA / Math.sqrt(vP);
  return {name, k, perCycle, perYear: perCycle / y, y};
}
A = scheme("Scheme A", pA, cA, yA)
B = scheme("Scheme B", pB, cB, yB)

md`| | *k* | Gain per cycle | Years per cycle | **Gain per year** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Scheme A | ${A.k.toFixed(2)} | ${A.perCycle.toFixed(2)} | ${A.y} | **${A.perYear.toFixed(2)}** |
| Scheme B | ${B.k.toFixed(2)} | ${B.perCycle.toFixed(2)} | ${B.y} | **${B.perYear.toFixed(2)}** |`
```

```{ojs}
cumulative = [A, B].flatMap(s => d3.range(0, 13).map(year => ({
  scheme: s.name, year, gain: Math.floor(year / s.y) * s.perCycle
})))

Plot.plot({
  height: 300,
  marginLeft: 50,
  x: {label: "Years", ticks: 12},
  y: {label: "Cumulative gain", grid: true},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Scheme A", "Scheme B"], range: [pal[0], pal[1]]},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(cumulative, {x: "year", y: "gain", stroke: "scheme", strokeWidth: 2, curve: "step-after"}),
    Plot.text(cumulative.filter(d => d.year === 12), {x: "year", y: "gain", text: "scheme", fill: "currentColor", dx: 6, textAnchor: "start"}),
    Plot.tip(cumulative, Plot.pointer({x: "year", y: "gain", stroke: "scheme", title: d => `${d.scheme}, year ${d.year}\ncumulative gain ${d.gain.toFixed(2)}`}))
  ],
  marginRight: 70
})
```

Gain arrives in steps, when each cycle is completed.

## Things to try

- Scheme B starts out like mass selection after pollination: one year per cycle but parental control ½. Set Scheme A to 3 years per cycle and B pulls ahead, despite gaining less than half as much per cycle.
- Hold everything equal except years per cycle. Halving cycle length doubles gain per year, which is often the cheapest lever a breeder has.
